definition: Pretext means a reason given to justify an action that is not the real reason — a cover story or invented excuse.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word pretext. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know pretext should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The spy entered the ballroom under the pretext of delivering flowers, when his true goal was to photograph the ambassador's guest list.
Excuse is weaker: an excuse may be honest, just feeble, while a pretext is a stated reason deliberately hiding the real one.
Ruse is stronger: a ruse is a full trick or scheme in action, while a pretext is only the false reason offered at the start.

A cover is whatever hides a real purpose — a front business, a fake job title, an assumed role. It can be a thing, an identity, or a story. A pretext is narrower: specifically the stated reason someone gives for acting. The spy's florist van is his cover; 'delivering flowers' is his pretext.

An alibi is a defensive claim that you were somewhere else when something happened, offered after the fact to clear yourself of blame. A pretext works before the act: it is the false reason given in advance to justify doing something. An alibi answers an accusation; a pretext opens a door.

A smokescreen is anything thrown up to obscure what is really going on — a flurry of statistics, a manufactured controversy. It hides by confusing and distracting. A pretext hides by explaining: it hands people a tidy false reason so that they stop looking for the real one.
